units.title: Work types, threads, processes, async tasks and the GIL
outcomes: Choose threads, processes or async tasks from CPU work, I/O waits, shared state and cancellation needs.
Measure CPU-bound thread scaling on default and free-threaded CPython 3.14 builds without assuming their GIL state.
Identify a blocking call that prevents other event-loop tasks from progressing.
units.why: Concurrency overlaps work; it does not automatically make that work parallel. A workload and build-specific experiment is a better design input than a blanket claim about Python threads.

next.note: Protect the state your chosen model shares.

study.title: Free-threaded CPython is a separate build
study.locator: Identifying free-threaded Python; The global interpreter lock in free-threaded Python; Thread safety; Performance characteristics

study.title: Process startup is part of the experiment
study.locator: Contexts and start methods: spawn, fork and forkserver, including the 3.14 default changes and safe importing of the main module

focus: Default CPython 3.14 has a GIL. Pure Python CPU loops do not gain multicore parallelism from its threads; I/O waits and native code that releases the GIL are different cases.

Free-threaded builds can execute Python threads in parallel. Record sys.version, sysconfig.get_config_var('Py_GIL_DISABLED') and sys._is_gil_enabled() after imports; an unsupported extension can re-enable the GIL.
Async tasks share an event-loop thread and yield cooperatively. A synchronous CPU loop or time.sleep inside a task stalls that loop.

Processes isolate state but pay startup and serialization costs. In 3.14 fork is no longer the default anywhere; supported POSIX platforms default to forkserver. Select and report the context explicitly.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, sum integers with a Python for-loop for four equal jobs of 5,000,000 iterations. Assert each result equals n*(n-1)//2. Compare serial, four threads and four spawned processes on both CPython 3.14 builds. Use one warm-up and five measured trials per mode, include pool startup and save raw times, CPU, full version and GIL state. A reference run on Intel Core i9-12900K gave median seconds serial/threads/processes of 0.304/0.321/0.153 on 3.14.4 default and 0.315/0.088/0.156 on 3.14.6 free-threaded with GIL disabled. These are observations, not required speedups. Also schedule a heartbeat around a synchronous blocking call, then replace it with an awaited nonblocking operation and explain the missing versus advancing heartbeat.
traps: Treating a free-threaded executable name as proof that the GIL stayed disabled after imports.
Replacing the loop with sum(range(n)) and calling it the same pure Python workload, or comparing different total work across worker counts.
Calling asyncio.to_thread a CPU-parallelism guarantee on the default build. It keeps blocking I/O off the loop but does not remove the GIL.

selfTest.q: Which model fits many socket waits with little CPU work?
selfTest.a: Async tasks fit when the client APIs are nonblocking. Threads fit blocking clients. Bound either model's in-flight work.

selfTest.q: Why might processes lose on tiny jobs?
selfTest.a: Startup, serialization and communication can cost more than the CPU work they parallelize.

selfTest.q: Does no GIL mean no need for locks?
selfTest.a: No. Internal container protection does not make a multi-step application invariant atomic.

selfTest.q: Do these two build measurements isolate the cost of removing the GIL?
selfTest.a: No. Patch versions and compilers differ too. Compare scaling within each build; do not attribute every cross-build timing difference to the GIL.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: matched-work concurrency comparisons and an event-loop blocking fault in the bounded worker pipeline.
units.stopWhen: You have correctness-checked raw timings from both builds and can justify a model for CPU work, blocking I/O and cancellation-sensitive work without claiming a universal speedup.

fit.note: Kept the model first pass and the pool's current Python reference; the latter qualifies default-build GIL claims and supplies 3.14 process-start behavior.

units.title: Synchronization primitives and concurrency hazards
outcomes: Protect a compound invariant with a lock and coordinate a bounded queue with condition predicates.
Reproduce a lost update and a deadlock with controlled interleavings, then remove their causes.
Distinguish deadlock, livelock, starvation and lost notification from slow useful work.
units.why: Correct shared-state code needs both safety and progress. A lucky stress run proves neither; force the interleaving that breaks the invariant.

study.title: Design Thread-Safe Blocking Queue
study.locator: Problem Statement, Required Operations, Concurrency Challenges and Approach 1: Single Lock with Conditions
study.depth: Stop before Approach 2. Python locks do not promise the fair-lock starvation guarantee shown in the analysis table.

focus: A lock protects an invariant across all its reads and writes. A semaphore counts admission permits; it does not by itself protect the buffer mutation.
Check the predicate under the condition's lock and wait in a loop. wait releases that lock while sleeping and reacquires it before returning; notify does not release it.
Remove circular lock acquisition with a global lock order. Livelock changes state without useful progress; starvation denies one participant progress while others advance.
Use barriers and events to control test schedules. A timeout detects a stuck test; it does not identify the underlying wait cycle.
units.reproduce: Force two threads to read the same counter before either writes using a Barrier(2) between read and write. After both join, assert 1 instead of the intended 2 on both default and free-threaded builds. Remove that barrier from the critical section, lock the full read-modify-write and assert 2. In a separate test, give two threads opposite first locks, synchronize them at a barrier and use timed second acquisitions to demonstrate the wait cycle without leaving hung threads. Then use one global lock order and assert both finish.
traps: Waiting while holding an unrelated lock needed by the notifier. Condition.wait releases only its own lock.
Putting the test barrier inside the repaired critical section. The first thread then waits for a second thread that cannot enter.
Assuming mutex or condition wakeups are FIFO. Python gives no general starvation-freedom guarantee.

selfTest.q: Why use while rather than if around Condition.wait?
selfTest.a: A wakeup does not reserve the resource. Another participant may consume it before this thread reacquires the lock.

selfTest.q: Does notify preserve a message for a future waiter?
selfTest.a: No. Persistent state is the predicate; check and update it under the same lock used by wait.

selfTest.q: When can empty and full semaphore counts sum to less than capacity?
selfTest.a: After a producer or consumer acquires a permit but before it releases the opposite permit. Reserved in-flight permits are missing from that sum.

selfTest.q: What does a fixed lock order prevent, and what does it not promise?
selfTest.a: It prevents a circular wait among those locks if all paths obey it. It does not guarantee fairness, bounded latency or freedom from other waits.

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Design Thread-Safe Blocking Queue
practice.locator: Problem Statement: put, take, offer, poll, peek and size; Approach 1: Single Lock with Conditions
practice.note: Implement the single-lock design in Python. Test capacity one, blocked producer and consumer, FIFO order and unique item delivery with events rather than sleeps. Do not claim Java-style thread interruption or fair-lock guarantees for Python.

units.stopWhen: Your controlled tests expose the lost update and wait cycle, the repairs pass, and the blocking queue preserves its capacity and delivery invariants with multiple producers and consumers.

fit.note: Kept the pool's primitives, hazards and named blocking-queue design. Restricted the Java-oriented solution to one lock and checked its Python semantics against threading.
